profile.reading:
Per PeeringDB's facility record for QTS Phoenix (PHX1), corroborated by QTS's own US-locations page, this facility sits at 120 E Van Buren St, Suite C130/200, Phoenix, AZ 85004, a downtown carrier-hotel building hosting the Ninja-IX Phoenix internet exchange (58 networks as of PeeringDB's last update) and connecting networks including Uber Technologies and Zayo.

QTS was founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas, and was taken private in a roughly $10 billion Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT)-led acquisition completed August 31, 2021, per Blackstone's own press release; QTS is no longer an independent SEC filer.

QTS positions itself as a "hyperscale-neutral" wholesale and colocation landlord, leasing built data center capacity to enterprise, cloud, and hyperscale tenants rather than operating its own end-user cloud service, a business model it shares with peers such as Digital Realty and CyrusOne. Since Blackstone completed its roughly $10 billion take-private acquisition in August 2021, QTS has continued expanding across multiple US metros rather than slowing development, including major campus filings and expansions in Phoenix (a 750MW, 375-acre Glendale campus acquired for $255.3 million in July 2022) and Dallas-Fort Worth (its two mega-scale Irving and Fort Worth campuses), consistent with the scale of buildout QTS has also pursued in Northern Virginia, Georgia, and Ohio, tracked elsewhere in this registry.

QTS was originally founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas by Chad Williams, and grew through a mix of acquisitions and ground-up construction into a national wholesale/colocation platform before its 2013 IPO as a publicly traded REIT; that public period ended with the 2021 Blackstone take-private deal. profile.reading:

The land was previously farmland that had also drawn interest from Oceanic Data Centers (approved 2020) and Facebook (which considered the site in 2018 before choosing Newton County, Georgia instead).

Georgia Power, the state's dominant investor-owned electric utility, has flagged data center load growth in its own integrated resource plan filings with state regulators as a major driver of future generation and transmission investment, a pattern also seen among Northern Virginia's Dominion Energy and Texas's ERCOT grid operator elsewhere in this registry. Metro Atlanta's data center growth has also drawn legislative attention over sales-tax exemptions for data center equipment, a policy debate covered in Georgia trade and political press as the industry has expanded across Fulton, Gwinnett, Fayette, and neighboring counties.

American Electric Power made substantial investments around 2010 establishing electrical substations and redundant heavy transmission infrastructure specifically to support the park's power demands, and New Albany structured deals requiring minimum annual payments from data center operators in exchange for partial property-tax abatement. The American Prospect, in a March 2026 feature on Ohio's data center growth ("Hollow Promises in Ohio's Silicon Heartland"), examined the gap between promised local economic benefits (jobs, tax revenue) and the industry's actual employment footprint once facilities are operational, alongside rising residential electricity costs tied to grid investment for data center demand, a critical counterpoint to the more promotional framing common in economic-development announcements; that reporting was not used here to source any specific operational fact about QTS's own New Albany buildings, but is noted as relevant regional context for a boom this registry documents across multiple operators (Google, Meta, and Amazon Web Services all also operate New Albany-area facilities tracked elsewhere in this registry).

Per Blackstone's own press release, Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT) and other Blackstone-affiliated funds completed a roughly $10 billion acquisition of QTS Realty Trust on August 31, 2021, taking the company private at $78 per share; QTS is no longer an independent SEC filer. QTS's Virginia campuses sit within this same regional grid and policy environment as neighboring hyperscale and colocation buildings operated by Amazon, Equinix, Digital Realty, and CyrusOne, all tracked elsewhere in this registry.

QTS positions itself as a "hyperscale-neutral" wholesale and colocation landlord, leasing built capacity to enterprise, cloud, and hyperscale tenants rather than operating its own end-user cloud service, a business model shared with peers like Digital Realty and CyrusOne in this same Northern Virginia corridor; under Blackstone ownership since 2021, QTS has continued expanding its US footprint (including its Manassas and Richmond 3 campuses, both still under construction as of the facts recorded here) rather than slowing development after going private.

reading:
QTS, legally QTS Realty Trust, LLC, was founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas, and went private in a Blackstone acquisition completed August 31, 2021, when Blackstone Infrastructure Partners and its non-traded REIT BREIT paid approximately $10 billion, $78 per share, for the company. It is no longer an independent SEC filer, its prior public CIK, 1577368, now covers only historical pre-acquisition filings.

The company's operator domain, qtsdatacenters.com, now redirects to q.com, whose site lists a US headquarters at 22271 Broderick Drive, Sterling, Virginia, an operations support center in Suwanee, Georgia, and an international office in London. The site describes the portfolio only loosely, as "30+ facilities across North America and Europe," while a secondary Wikipedia summary puts the figure at 28 data center locations across 16 US states and two Netherlands sites, Eemshaven and Groningen, a page whose count and the operator's own site do not fully agree.

The registry here tracks 54 QTS facilities across ten states, Arizona, California, Colorado, Georgia, Illinois, New Jersey, Ohio, Oregon, Texas, and Virginia. As a Blackstone-owned private colocation operator, QTS sits in this registry's colocation and wholesale-landlord category rather than its hyperscaler category, alongside Digital Realty, leasing built capacity to enterprise and cloud tenants rather than running its own end-user compute or cloud service. No megawatt capacity figure or dollar-denominated US construction investment total was located in the sources reviewed this session.
